title: Application-Layer Protocols
summary: The protocols your apps actually speak: HTTP, email, file transfer, SSH, DHCP, and more — with their ports, transport choices, and why each one exists.

blocks.markdown:
The **application layer** (Layer 7) is the top of the [osi-tcpip-models](osi-tcpip-models) stack. It provides the language apps use to talk over the network.

- Defines **message format**, request/response rules, and error codes for each service.
- Relies on [transport-layer](transport-layer) TCP or UDP to actually move bytes — it doesn't care about routing.
- One protocol per job: HTTP for web, SMTP for email, SSH for shells, DHCP for addresses.

blocks.subTitle: Protocol quick-reference
blocks.markdown:
Common protocols at a glance.

| Protocol | Port | Transport |
|---|---|---|
| HTTP / HTTPS | 80 / 443 | TCP |
| SMTP | 25 / 587 | TCP |
| IMAP | 143 / 993 | TCP |
| POP3 | 110 / 995 | TCP |
| FTP | 21 (ctrl) / 20 (data) | TCP |
| SFTP / SSH | 22 | TCP |
| Telnet | 23 | TCP |
| DHCP | 67 / 68 | UDP |
| SNMP | 161 / 162 | UDP |

**HTTP** (HyperText Transfer Protocol) is the request/response protocol browsers and servers use to transfer web pages and APIs.

- Client sends a **request** (GET, POST, …); server returns a **response** with a status code (200 OK, 404 Not Found).
- **HTTPS** is HTTP over **TLS** (Transport Layer Security) — same messages, encrypted tunnel.
- Port **80** (HTTP) and **443** (HTTPS); both use TCP.

HTTP/HTTPS gets its own deep topic at [http-https](http-https) — this is the overview.

blocks.subTitle: Sending vs retrieving
blocks.markdown:
Three protocols divide email work:

- **SMTP** (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) — sends mail from client to server and between servers. Port **25** (server-to-server) or **587** (client submission).
- **IMAP** (Internet Message Access Protocol) — read mail on the server; messages stay there; sync across devices. Port **143**.
- **POP3** (Post Office Protocol 3) — download mail to one device and delete from server. Port **110**.

All three use TCP.

blocks.subTitle: SMTP vs IMAP vs POP3
blocks.markdown:
Choosing the right email protocol:

- **SMTP** — always for sending. Never for reading.
- **IMAP** — best for multiple devices (phone + laptop); server holds the source of truth.
- **POP3** — useful only when you want one local copy and low server storage.

Gmail/Outlook use SMTP to send and IMAP to sync.

**FTP** (File Transfer Protocol) moves files between client and server using **two TCP connections**: port **21** for commands (control channel) and port **20** for the actual file data.

- No encryption — credentials travel in plaintext.
- **SFTP** (SSH File Transfer Protocol) tunnels file transfer through SSH on port **22** — fully encrypted, single connection.
- Use SFTP (or FTPS = FTP + TLS) in any modern setting; plain FTP only on isolated internal networks.

blocks.subTitle: SSH
blocks.markdown:
**SSH** (Secure Shell) gives you an encrypted remote terminal — you type commands on your laptop, they run on the remote server.

- Port **22**, TCP.
- Authentication via password or **public-key cryptography** (preferred).
- Also used as a secure tunnel for SFTP and port-forwarding.

SSH is the standard for all remote server administration today.

blocks.subTitle: Telnet
blocks.markdown:
**Telnet** is the legacy remote-terminal protocol that predates SSH. Port **23**, TCP.

- Sends everything — including passwords — as **plaintext**. Anyone sniffing the network can read it.
- Replaced by SSH in all production environments.
- Still occasionally used to **test TCP port connectivity**: `telnet host 80` checks whether port 80 is open.

Never use Telnet for real remote access.

blocks.subTitle: What DHCP does
blocks.markdown:
**DHCP** (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) automatically assigns IP addresses to devices when they join a network — no manual config needed.

- Runs over **UDP**, ports **67** (server) and **68** (client).
- Why UDP? The client has no IP yet when it starts — TCP needs an IP to establish a connection, so UDP broadcasts are used instead.
- Assigns: IP address, subnet mask, default gateway, DNS server.

blocks.subTitle: The DORA handshake
blocks.markdown:
DHCP assigns an IP in four broadcast steps — **DORA**:

1. **Discover** — client broadcasts "any DHCP server out there?"
2. **Offer** — server replies with an available IP lease offer.
3. **Request** — client broadcasts "I'd like that IP" (also tells other servers it chose one).
4. **Acknowledge** — server confirms the lease, including duration.

The lease expires after a set time; the client renews it before expiry.

**SNMP** (Simple Network Management Protocol) lets network management software monitor and control routers, switches, servers, and other devices.

- Port **161** (queries from manager to device), **162** (traps — unsolicited alerts sent by device). UDP.
- An SNMP **agent** runs on each managed device; a **manager** polls agents for stats (CPU, bandwidth, errors).
- **Trap**: device proactively alerts the manager about an event (link down, threshold exceeded).
- SNMPv3 added authentication and encryption; v1/v2 are plaintext.

blocks.sectionTitle: TCP vs UDP at the application layer
blocks.markdown:
Why each protocol picks its transport:

- **TCP** — chosen when correctness matters: web pages, email, file transfers, remote shells. Retransmits lost packets.
- **UDP** — chosen when low latency beats reliability: DHCP (no IP yet), SNMP (fire-and-forget polls), DNS lookups, video streaming.

Rule of thumb: if losing a message is tolerable or the app handles retries itself, UDP wins on speed. See [transport-layer](transport-layer).

blocks.subTitle: Port numbers
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What ports do HTTPS, SSH, and DNS use?**

**HTTPS** → 443 (TCP). **SSH** → 22 (TCP). **DNS** → 53 (UDP for queries, TCP for zone transfers).

Know the full set: HTTP 80, SMTP 25/587, IMAP 143, POP3 110, FTP 21, Telnet 23, DHCP 67/68, SNMP 161.

blocks.subTitle: SMTP vs IMAP vs POP3
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What's the difference between SMTP, IMAP, and POP3?**

**SMTP** sends mail (client→server, server→server). **IMAP** reads mail while leaving it on the server — syncs across devices. **POP3** downloads mail to one device and removes it from the server.

You always need SMTP to send; IMAP is preferred for reading on modern multi-device setups.

blocks.subTitle: DHCP DORA & Telnet insecurity
blocks.markdown:
**Q: How does DHCP assign an IP? And why is Telnet insecure?**

**DHCP DORA**: Discover (client broadcast) → Offer (server proposes IP) → Request (client accepts) → Acknowledge (server confirms lease). Uses UDP because the client has no IP yet.

**Telnet**: sends all traffic — passwords included — as plaintext over the wire. Any attacker who can sniff the network segment reads everything. SSH replaced it by encrypting the full session.
